entries.title: What GMDSS Is and Why It Is Needed
commentary: GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is a global communication system, mandatory under SOLAS (Chapter IV) for all passenger ships and cargo ships of 300 gross tonnage and above engaged on international voyages.

Its purpose is to guarantee that a distress signal reaches shore and nearby ships from virtually any point of the world's oceans, rather than relying solely on voice radio communication and a watchkeeper's hearing.

The key idea of the system: instead of a person listening to the airwaves 24 hours a day, equipment (DSC, satellite) automatically receives and relays the alert signal, and automatic determination of the ship's position (via GPS) is included in the distress alert straight away.

GMDSS composition: shipborne and shore-based DSC equipment (VHF/MF/HF), satellite communication (Inmarsat, COSPAS-SARSAT), NAVTEX, EPIRBs, radar transponders (SART/AIS-SART), and VHF radiotelephones for on-scene communication at the distress location.

entries.title: Sea Areas A1–A4
entries.example: A ship in the Baltic Sea is normally within A1/A2 for the whole voyage. A ship crossing the Atlantic spends most of the passage in A3. A ship in the high latitudes of the Arctic may find itself in A4, where there is no geostationary satellite coverage.
commentary: For GMDSS purposes, the world is divided into 4 sea areas, which determine what equipment must be carried on board a ship.
A1 — within the coverage of at least one shore-based VHF station providing continuous DSC coverage (typically 20–30 miles from shore, depending on the administration of the area).
A2 — outside A1, but within the coverage of at least one shore-based MF station providing continuous DSC coverage (typically up to about 100 miles from shore).

A3 — outside A1 and A2, but within the coverage of a recognized mobile satellite service supported by the ship earth station carried on board (SOLAS chapter IV as amended, in force from 1 January 2024). For Inmarsat this is roughly 70°N — 70°S; Iridium coverage is global.

A4 — everything outside A1, A2 and A3. For a ship with an Inmarsat station these are the polar waters beyond geostationary coverage, where long-range communication is HF DSC. Narrow-band direct printing (radiotelex, NBDP) is no longer mandatory since 2024.

entries.title: Mandatory Equipment by Sea Area (General Principle)
commentary: The exact mandatory equipment fit for a particular ship is determined by the classification society/register based on its intended area of operation — this is only the general principle, not a ready-made checklist.

The further the area of operation is from shore, the more communication means are required in a redundant manner (VHF DSC for A1, MF DSC is added for A2, a recognized mobile satellite service station (Inmarsat or Iridium) or MF/HF for A3, MF/HF DSC for A4).

Regardless of the area, a GMDSS ship must carry: a VHF DSC station, a NAVTEX receiver (within the coverage of NAVTEX transmitters), a 406 MHz EPIRB, a radar transponder (SART or AIS-SART, at least 1–2 units depending on gross tonnage), and portable VHF radios for survival craft.

entries.title: What MMSI Is and Its Structure
entries.example: MMSI of the form 273123456: 273 is Russia's MID, 123456 is the ship's sequential number.
commentary: MMSI (Maritime Mobile Service Identity) — a unique 9-digit numerical identifier of a ship (or shore) radio station, used in DSC, AIS and the digital part of satellite communication.

The first 3 digits of a ship station's MMSI are the flag/registry country code, the MID (Maritime Identification Digits) — for example, 273 is Russia; the specific set of MIDs is periodically expanded by IMO/ITU.
The remaining 6 digits are a sequential number assigned by the country's communications administration to a specific ship.

A ship's MMSI is physically programmed into the memory of the DSC radio station and the AIS transponder — an officer of the watch normally cannot change it in ordinary operating mode (special service access is required, to prevent accidental corruption of the number).

entries.title: MMSI Formats for Different Station Types
commentary: Ship station: 9 digits, beginning with the MID (e.g. 273XXXXXX).
Coast station: begins with 00, followed by the MID, followed by 4 digits (00 + MID + XXXX).
Group call (for a fleet belonging to one company/group of ships): begins with 0 (not 00), followed by the MID, followed by 5 digits (0 + MID + XXXXX).
Search and rescue aircraft (SAR aircraft): begins with 111, followed by the MID, followed by 3 digits (111 + MID + XXX).
Aid to navigation fitted with AIS (AIS AtoN — e.g. a buoy with an AIS beacon): begins with 99, followed by the MID, followed by 4 digits (99 + MID + XXXX).

entries.title: What DSC Is and What Frequencies It Uses
commentary: DSC (Digital Selective Calling) — a method of automatically transmitting a short digital packet (a call/alert with MMSI, coordinates, and nature of distress), rather than voice.
VHF DSC — working channel 70 (156.525 MHz), reserved ONLY for DSC (not for voice) — after contact is established via DSC, communication switches to a voice channel (usually channel 16).
MF DSC — frequency 2187.5 kHz.
HF DSC — several designated frequencies across different bands (used depending on propagation conditions and time of day).

A ship's DSC receiver continuously "listens" on the calling channel in the background, even while the watchkeeper is engaged in voice communication on another channel — this is what ensures round-the-clock readiness to receive an alert.

entries.title: Procedure for Sending a Distress Alert via DSC
commentary: A DSC station has a separate protected "Distress" button (usually under a hinged cover, to prevent accidental activation).

Holding the button (typically for a few seconds — the exact time is set by the instructions for the specific station model) initiates transmission of the DSC distress alert to all ships/shore within range.

The alert automatically includes: the ship's MMSI, position and time (taken from a connected GPS receiver, if one is fitted and connected), and, optionally, the nature of distress (selected in advance from a list) and the last known course/speed.

After sending the DSC distress alert, the ship must switch to voice communication (VHF channel 16 or 2182 kHz MF) and transmit a voice MAYDAY message with the ship's name, call sign, position and nature of distress, and must also switch on the receiver to listen for an acknowledgement.
The DSC distress alert is automatically repeated by the station at set intervals until an acknowledgement is received (or it is manually stopped by the watchkeeper).

entries.title: False Distress Alert — Cancellation Procedure
commentary: Accidental activation of the Distress button (a common practical occurrence, especially among cadets/new crew members) requires IMMEDIATE cancellation — it must not simply be ignored in the hope that it will "go away by itself", as it puts all nearby ships and shore services on alert.

Procedure: (1) as quickly as possible, transmit a voice cancellation in plain language on VHF channel 16 (or 2182 kHz MF): "All stations, all stations, all stations, this is [ship's name/call sign], cancel my distress alert of [time] [date], position [...], nature of distress — false activation".
(2) If the station supports a DSC distress cancellation/all ships routine call function with an explanation, send it in addition to the voice message.
(3) Where possible, contact the nearest coast station/MRCC directly and report the error separately.

False alerts are a well-known, practically frequent GMDSS problem (accidental button presses, programming errors during commissioning) — what matters is not that it happened, but how quickly and correctly it is cancelled.

entries.title: EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon)
commentary: EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) — an autonomous distress beacon that transmits a distress signal via the COSPAS-SARSAT satellite system on 406 MHz.

It activates automatically on release from its hydrostatic release unit if the ship sinks (mounted on a special bracket, released hydrostatically at a depth of a few metres), or it can be activated manually/remotely.
It also has a low-power homing beacon on 121.5 MHz for precise direction-finding by survival craft during the final stage of a search.

The 406 MHz signal encoding contains an identifier (usually the MMSI or a separate beacon registration number) — when the beacon is registered in a national register, the ship's details and verification contacts are linked to that number, which greatly speeds up the response of the search and rescue services.

Requires periodic testing (the battery and hydrostatic release unit have a limited service life — typically several years, the exact interval is stated in the beacon's manual) — check against your ship's maintenance schedule.

entries.title: SART and AIS-SART (Radar Transponders)
commentary: SART (Search and Rescue Transponder) — a classic X-band (9 GHz) radar transponder: when illuminated by a searching ship's radar, it responds with a series of 12 characteristic dots along the bearing on the searching ship's radar display — this is how a search vessel locates those in distress even without visual contact.

AIS-SART — a newer type that, instead of responding to radar, transmits its own AIS messages, which appear as a distinct mark on the AIS/ECDIS display of searching ships — it does not require the search to be conducted specifically by radar.
Both types are part of the survival craft equipment (usually fitted to liferafts/lifeboats) and are switched on manually when the survival craft is used.
Range is limited primarily by the height of the searching ship's antenna above the water (radio horizon) — in practice, a few miles.

entries.title: NAVTEX
commentary: NAVTEX — a system for automatic reception of navigational warnings and other navigationally significant information (MSI — Maritime Safety Information: storm warnings, ice conditions, notices to mariners, etc.) via narrow-band teleprinter.
The international frequency 518 kHz — broadcasts in English; the frequency 490 kHz — in the coastal state's national language (where provided).
Reception range from a single shore station is roughly 200–400 miles (the exact figure depends on transmitter power and propagation conditions).

A NAVTEX receiver can be set to accept messages only from the desired stations and message categories (letter codes for message type — for example, A for navigational warnings, B for meteorological warnings, etc.), so as not to overload the watch with irrelevant information.

entries.title: Satellite Communication (Inmarsat and Others)
commentary: Inmarsat — a system of geostationary communication satellites, providing voice communication, telex/data, and a dedicated distress button on terminals aboard ships within sea area A3 (approximately 70°N – 70°S).

Different Inmarsat terminals (e.g. Fleet, FleetBroadband, and others) differ in data transmission speed and operating cost — the specific type of station carried on a ship is determined by the requirements of its area of operation and the shipowner's fit-out.
In high latitudes, where Inmarsat geostationary satellites are below the horizon, the primary long-range channel for an Inmarsat-equipped ship is HF DSC.

Since 2020 IMO has recognized Iridium (a low-earth-orbit constellation with global coverage, including the polar regions) as a GMDSS service provider alongside Inmarsat. From 1 January 2024 SOLAS chapter IV refers to a “recognized mobile satellite service” instead of Inmarsat — check the ship's Record of Equipment for the station actually fitted.
